text: When someone asks a yes-or-no question and you're not sure, you'll be able to answer in a few words: penso di sì, credo di no. You'll also hear penso che è in relaxed speech, but careful speakers use the subjunctive.
why: The second sentence slips in a second point (penso che è versus penso che sia) that no example, notice or practice shows, and it steers the learner away from a form instead of teaching the one this lesson is about: short answers with di sì / di no.
fix: When someone asks a yes-or-no question and you're not sure, you'll be able to answer in a few words: penso di sì, credo di no, spero di sì.

text: Anche se piove, vado a correre. / Even if it rains, I'm going running.
why: The lesson teaches 'even though' (doing something despite a reason not to), but the English makes this a hypothetical 'even if', a different meaning, so the example doesn't show the point and blurs the notice's 'both mean even though'.
fix: said: "Anche se piove, vado a correre lo stesso." en: "Even though it's raining, I'm going running anyway."
